headline: Drought Unearths 350-Year-Old Garden Hidden Beneath British Estate
meta_description: A record heatwave in Derbyshire exposed the intricate design of a 17th-century formal garden buried for centuries at Chatsworth House.
summary_short: Extreme heat and drought at Chatsworth House in Derbyshire have temporarily revealed the hidden outlines of an ornate 17th-century garden beneath the lawn.
body:
A severe heatwave sweeping across England this summer has inadvertently restored a piece of lost history. At Chatsworth House in Derbyshire, record temperatures exceeding 30°C (86°F) combined with exceptionally dry conditions have caused the modern lawn to parch in revealing patterns—exposing the ornate geometry of a formal garden that disappeared more than 350 years ago. The intricate design, known as 'The Great Parterre', was originally created around 1699 for the 1st Duke of Devonshire and stretched 473 feet long by 227 feet wide across the south façade of the estate. This elaborate, perfectly symmetrical arrangement of flower beds and paths followed the fashion of formal gardens at the time, only to be covered over and replaced with a new design around 1730.

The reason the ancient garden pattern becomes visible during drought is elegantly simple. Because the replacement grass has shallower roots than the original flower beds and pathways beneath it, the lawn burns more quickly under intense heat and dry conditions. This creates a natural contrast that temporarily traces the swirling outlines of the Duke's original design—a ghostly reminder of Chatsworth's horticultural past.

Now home to the Devonshire family for 16 generations, the estate maintains 105 acres of gardens, with the rediscovered parterre now comprising the south lawn. What might otherwise be remembered as merely a difficult growing season has instead become an unexpected window into the estate's rich heritage, allowing gardeners and historians alike to witness a design that thrived for only three decades before being consciously abandoned for the fashions of a new era.
quick_facts: Record heatwave in May, June, July exceeded 30°C in Derbyshire
'The Great Parterre' measured 473 feet by 227 feet
Garden was created around 1699, covered over by 1730
Shallow-rooted replacement grass reveals pattern when parched
Part of 105-acre garden at historic Chatsworth House
